title: cfeasy
text:
cfeasy is for people who host their own services on a server and use Cloudflare for the domain. It does two jobs. It writes DNS records, the entries that say where a name like app.example.com points. And it sets up Cloudflare Tunnels, which let visitors reach a service on your server without opening any ports on it.
Cloudflare publishes an official Python SDK that can do all of this, but each job takes several calls and you have to look up zone and account IDs yourself. cfeasy wraps the SDK in one class, CF, whose methods take domain and tunnel names and find the IDs for you. The examples on this page ran against a real Cloudflare account; they are marked so that the docs build does not run them again.

title: cfeasy
text:
Create an API token
cfeasy talks to Cloudflare with an API token. It needs a custom token, which you create with only the permissions you choose. The older Global API Key, which can do anything on the account, does not work with it.
Open dash.cloudflare.com/profile/api-tokens, choose Create Token, then Custom Token, and add these three permissions:








What it is for
Resource
Permission




Reading and writing DNS records
Zone -> DNS
Edit (limit it to your zone)


Finding your account ID
Account -> Account Settings
Read


Creating and deleting tunnels
Account -> Cloudflare Tunnel
Edit






Cloudflare custom token setup

title: cfeasy
text:
Connect and check the token
CF takes the token as its first argument. If you leave it out, the SDK reads it from the CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN environment variable, which keeps the token out of your code.
Before changing anything, call verify. It only reads: it looks up your account, lists your zones (a zone is a domain you manage on Cloudflare) and lists your tunnels. It also checks that the token is active. It returns ok, the token status, the account ID, the zone names and the tunnel count. If a check fails, usually because the token is expired or lacks one of the permissions above, ok is False and errors holds Cloudflare’s message for each failed check. Pass domain to check one zone instead of listing them all.

from cfeasy import *


c = CF()  # set CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN env var and just do CF() or pass a token directly CF('your-token-here')
# Confirm your token has the right permissions before doing anything
c.verify()  # → {'ok': True, 'token': 'active', ...}

{'ok': True,
 'token': 'active',
 'account': '…',
 'zones': ['angalama.com'],
 'tunnels': 1,
 'errors': {}}

title: cfeasy
text:
DNS records
A DNS record tells the internet where a name such as app.angalama.com points. An A record holds an IPv4 address, and a CNAME record holds another name to look up instead.
upsert_record is the method to use for writing a record, because running it a second time leaves you with the same result instead of a duplicate. You give it the domain, the name, and the content. A name without a dot, such as app, is taken as a subdomain of the domain; a name with a dot is used as written. The record type defaults to A.
The method first looks at the records that already exist under that name. If one has the same type and content, it is returned as it is. Otherwise the old records under the name are deleted, whatever their type, and the new record is created. The example below points app.angalama.com at the address 1.2.3.4 and returns the record as Cloudflare stored it:

# A record pointing "app.angalama.com" at an IP
dom, nm = 'angalama.com', 'app'
c.upsert_record(dom, nm, "1.2.3.4")

title: cfeasy
text:
Tunnels
A Cloudflare Tunnel solves the problem of exposing a service on a server that you would rather not open to the internet. A small program called cloudflared runs next to your service and makes an outgoing connection to Cloudflare. When someone visits app.example.com, Cloudflare sends the request down that connection, and cloudflared passes it to your service. The server needs no open ports and no public IP address.
Three things have to exist for this to work:

A tunnel, registered with your Cloudflare account under a name you choose.
A CNAME record that points your subdomain at <tunnel-id>.cfargotunnel.com, the address Cloudflare gives every tunnel.
A tunnel token, a secret string you give to cloudflared so that it connects to the right tunnel.

The cell below makes each one by hand. tunnels lists the account’s tunnels, so the code reuses a tunnel called my-app if there is one and calls create_tunnel if not. tunnel_cname writes the CNAME record through upsert_record, with Cloudflare’s proxy turned on, which a tunnel needs. tunnel_token fetches the token.

# Step 1: create the tunnel
tname = 'my-app'
exists = L.filter(lambda x: x.get('name') == tname)
tid = first(t)['id'] if (t:=exists(c.tunnels())) else c.create_tunnel(tname)['id']
# Step 2: point the subdomain at it (CNAME → <tid>.cfargotunnel.com)
c.tunnel_cname(dom, nm, tid)
# Step 3: get the token for cloudflared
token = c.tunnel_token(tid)

title: cfeasy
section: Set up a tunnel in one call
text:
Set up a tunnel in one call
setup_tunnel does the three steps above for you, and it is the method to reach for unless you need to control each step. It returns the tunnel ID and the token. Pass the token to cloudflared, for example as the CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN environment variable that the cloudflared_svc service in the dockeasy package reads.
Give it a domain and a subdomain name to serve app.example.com, as in the first example. Leave the name out to serve the domain itself, as in the second. A CNAME record at the root of a domain is normally not allowed, but Cloudflare accepts it and resolves it to addresses on its side, which it calls CNAME flattening.
The tunnel is named after the subdomain, or after the domain when there is no subdomain; pass tunnel_name to choose another name. If a tunnel with that name already exists it is reused, so calling setup_tunnel again does not make a second one.

# Subdomain tunnel: app.example.com
tid, token = c.setup_tunnel(dom, nm)
tid, token


# Apex tunnel: example.com itself (no subdomain)
tid_apex, token_apex = c.setup_tunnel(dom)
tid_apex, token_apex

tunnel_id finds a tunnel’s ID from its name, which helps when you set a tunnel up earlier and kept only the name. setup_tunnel names a tunnel after its subdomain, or after the domain for an apex tunnel, so those are the names to look up. delete_tunnel removes a tunnel by ID; together the two clean up both tunnels made above. Deleting a tunnel leaves its CNAME record in place, so remove that with delete_record if you no longer need it.

# Look up a tunnel ID by name: useful when you only have the name, not the ID
c.tunnel_id(nm)          # → UUID for the "app" tunnel
c.tunnel_id(dom)         # → UUID for the apex tunnel


# Cleanup: delete by name instead of needing to track the ID
c.delete_tunnel(c.tunnel_id(nm))
c.delete_tunnel(c.tunnel_id(dom))

title: cfeasy
text:
Cache rules and purges
ruleset_upsert writes cache rules or custom firewall rules into a zone. It replaces your rules by their ref, keeps everyone else’s whole, and returns False when the zone already has them, so a deploy can run it every time. purge empties the cache by URL, by URL prefix or entirely. It retries rate limits and timeouts with backoff. If Cloudflare refuses a prefix purge on your plan, it purges everything instead and tells you so in its return value; any other error raises. Both need a token with the matching zone permissions: Cache Rules -> Edit, Zone WAF -> Edit for firewall rules, and Cache Purge -> Purge.

zid = c.zone_id(dom)
rule = dict(ref='static', expression='starts_with(http.request.uri.path, "/static/")', action='set_cache_settings',
            action_parameters=dict(cache=True), enabled=True)
c.ruleset_upsert(zid, [rule])                # True the first time, False after
c.purge(zid, prefixes=[f'{dom}/static/'])   # [{'prefixes': [...]}], or [{'purge_everything': True}] if refused

title: cloudflare
text:
CF holds one connection to the Cloudflare API and offers a method for each job. The token comes from the token argument, or from the CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN environment variable when you leave it out. timeout is the number of seconds to wait for each request, and any other keyword arguments go straight to the SDK’s Cloudflare client.
Every method returns plain dictionaries and lists, converted from the SDK’s objects, so the results print and serialise without extra work.
The methods come in three groups:

Zones and DNS records: zones, zone_id, dns_records, create_record, delete_record and upsert_record. A zone is a domain you manage on Cloudflare. The low-level methods take a zone ID; upsert_record takes the domain name and looks the ID up itself, so it is the one to use in most code.
Tunnels: account_id, tunnels, tunnel_id, create_tunnel, delete_tunnel, tunnel_token and tunnel_cname. Tunnels belong to an account rather than a zone, so tunnels, tunnel_id, create_tunnel, delete_tunnel and tunnel_token take an optional account_id and use your first account when you leave it out. tunnel_cname writes the DNS record that points a name at a tunnel.
Shortcuts: verify checks the token without changing anything, and setup_tunnel creates a tunnel, its DNS record and its token in one call.

upsert_record keeps one record per name. It walks the records that already have the name. The first one with the same type and content is kept and returned, and any record it passed on the way is deleted. If none match, every record under the name is deleted, whatever its type, and the new record is created. A name without a dot is treated as a subdomain of the domain.


source


def CF(
    token:NoneType=None, timeout:int=10, **kw
):
A Cloudflare API client for DNS records and tunnels, built on the official cloudflare SDK.




Give the token only the permissions cfeasy needs. Create a custom token in the Cloudflare dashboard under My Profile -> API Tokens -> Create Token:







What it is for
Permission




DNS records
Zone -> DNS -> Edit (limit it to your zone)


Finding the account ID for tunnel calls
Account -> Account Settings -> Read


Creating, listing and deleting tunnels
Account -> Cloudflare Tunnel -> Edit



verify confirms the token works before you change anything. It checks that the token is active, that it can see an account, its zones (or the one zone named by domain) and that account’s tunnels. It returns ok, the token status, the account ID, the zone names, the tunnel count and an errors dict naming each check that failed. Account-owned tokens are checked against the account endpoint. The examples below ran against a real account and are not run by the docs build. The second setup_tunnel call serves the domain sankalpa.sh itself instead of a subdomain.

from types import SimpleNamespace as NS
from unittest.mock import MagicMock
from fastcore.test import test_eq, test_fail


class Pg(list):
    "SDK pages are truthy even when empty."
    def __bool__(self): return True

def fake_cf(status='active', zones=('example.com',), accts=('acc1',), user_tok=True):
    c = CF('x'); m = c._c = MagicMock()
    v = NS(id='t1', status=status)
    if user_tok: m.user.tokens.verify.return_value = v
    else: m.user.tokens.verify.side_effect = Exception('Invalid API Token')
    m.accounts.tokens.verify.return_value = v
    m.accounts.list.side_effect = lambda: Pg(NS(id=a) for a in accts)
    m.zones.list.side_effect = lambda name=None: Pg(NS(id=f'z-{z}', name=z, model_dump=lambda z=z: dict(name=z)) for z in zones if name in (None, z))
    m.zero_trust.tunnels.cloudflared.list.side_effect = lambda account_id: Pg()
    return c


r = fake_cf().verify()
test_eq(r, dict(ok=True, token='active', account='acc1', zones=['example.com'], tunnels=0, errors={}))
r = fake_cf(status='disabled').verify()
test_eq((r['ok'], r['token'], list(r['errors'])), (False, 'disabled', ['token']))
r = fake_cf(zones=()).verify()
test_eq((r['ok'], list(r['errors'])), (False, ['zones']))
r = fake_cf().verify(domain='other.com')
test_eq((r['ok'], r['zones'], r['errors']['zones']), (False, None, 'Zone not found: other.com'))
test_eq(fake_cf().verify(domain='example.com')['zones'], ['example.com'])
r = fake_cf(accts=()).verify()
test_eq((r['ok'], r['account'], r['tunnels'], 'account' in r['errors']), (False, None, None, True))
test_eq(fake_cf(user_tok=False).verify()['token'], 'active')


c = CF()
c.verify()

{'result': True}



# setup_tunnel: subdomain
tid, token = c.setup_tunnel('sankalpa.sh', 'app')   # → app.sankalpa.sh
tid, token

A zone keeps its cache rules and its custom firewall rules in rulesets, one entrypoint ruleset per phase. ruleset_upsert puts your rules into the entrypoint for phase and keeps every rule there that it does not own, with all its keys, such as logging or ratelimit; only Cloudflare’s read-only version, last_updated and categories are left out of the update. A rule is matched by its ref, so give each rule a stable ref. When the rules with those refs already match yours on the usual keys and every key your rules set, it sends nothing and returns False; otherwise it writes the merged list and returns True. Running it on every deploy is safe. The token needs Zone -> Cache Rules -> Edit for the cache phase, and Zone -> Zone WAF -> Edit for http_request_firewall_custom.
purge empties the zone’s cache by URL files, by URL prefixes, or everything. Files and prefixes go in separate requests, files first, because the API takes one kind per request. A rate limit (HTTP 429 or Cloudflare’s code 1134) or a timeout is retried up to tries times in all, waiting wait seconds and doubling the wait each time. Some plans or tokens refuse a prefix purge, with HTTP 403 or a 400 that names the plan or a permission. With fallback_all=True, the default, such a refusal becomes a purge of everything. Any other error, including a rate limit that outlasts the retries, raises and purges nothing more. The return value lists the purge requests that succeeded: after a fallback, the files purge when it ran first, then the purge of everything, so a caller can tell when the fallback ran.


source


def purge(
    zid, prefixes:NoneType=None, files:NoneType=None, everything:bool=False, fallback_all:bool=True, tries:int=4,
    wait:int=1
)->list:
Purge the zone cache by files, prefixes or everything, retrying rate limits and timeouts, and purging everything when Cloudflare refuses a partial purge and fallback_all; returns the purges that succeeded.




source


def ruleset_upsert(
    zid, rules, phase:str='http_request_cache_settings'
)->bool:
Put rules in the zone entrypoint for phase, replacing the rules with the same ref and keeping the rest whole; False when nothing changed.



def fake_rules(rules=()):
    c, calls = CF('x'), []
    R = lambda d: NS(model_dump=lambda exclude_none=True: d)
    c._c = NS(rulesets=NS(phases=NS(get=lambda ph, zone_id: NS(rules=[R(r) for r in rules]),
                                    update=lambda ph, zone_id, rules: calls.append((ph, rules)))))
    return c, calls

mine = [dict(ref='a', expression='true', action='set_cache_settings', action_parameters=dict(cache=True), enabled=True)]
theirs = dict(id='o1', ref='theirs', expression='true', action='block', enabled=True, version='3', last_updated='2026-10-19T00:00:00Z',
              logging=dict(enabled=False), ratelimit=dict(characteristics=['ip.src'], period=60, requests_per_period=10))
c, calls = fake_rules([theirs, dict(mine[0], id='v1', expression='false')])
test_eq(c.ruleset_upsert('z', mine), True)
(ph, sent), = calls
test_eq((ph, [r['ref'] for r in sent]), ('http_request_cache_settings', ['theirs', 'a']))
test_eq(sent[0], {k: v for k, v in theirs.items() if k not in ('version', 'last_updated')})   # a rule it does not own keeps its whole body
assert 'version' not in sent[0]
c, calls = fake_rules([theirs, dict(mine[0], id='v1')])
test_eq((c.ruleset_upsert('z', mine, phase='http_request_firewall_custom'), calls), (False, []))
logged = [dict(mine[0], logging=dict(enabled=False))]
c, calls = fake_rules([dict(mine[0], id='v1')])
test_eq(c.ruleset_upsert('z', logged), True)   # a change to a key of its own beyond the usual ones is a change
bare = [dict(ref='b', expression='true', action='set_cache_settings', action_parameters=dict(cache=True), description=None)]
stored = dict(bare[0], id='v2', version='1', last_updated='2026-10-19T00:00:00Z', enabled=True, description='')   # the API fills both in
c, calls = fake_rules([stored])
test_eq((c.ruleset_upsert('z', bare), calls), (False, []))


import httpx
from unittest import mock
from cloudflare import APITimeoutError, BadRequestError, PermissionDeniedError, RateLimitError
_rq = httpx.Request('POST', 'https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/zones/z/purge_cache')
def cf_err(cls, status, code, msg): return cls(msg, response=httpx.Response(status, request=_rq), body=dict(errors=[dict(code=code, message=msg)]))
refused = lambda: cf_err(PermissionDeniedError, 403, 10000, 'not on this plan')
def fake_purge(fails=None):
    'A client whose purge raises, for each kind of purge in `fails`, the errors listed there in turn, then succeeds; `calls` records each request.'
    c, calls, fails = CF('x'), [], {k: list(v) for k, v in (fails or {}).items()}
    def purge(zone_id, **kw):
        calls.append(kw)
        if (q := fails.get(first(kw))) and (e := q.pop(0)()): raise e
    c._c = NS(cache=NS(purge=purge))
    return c, calls

c, calls = fake_purge()
test_eq(c.purge('z', prefixes=['e.com/s/'], files=['https://e.com/']), [dict(files=['https://e.com/']), dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/'])])
test_eq(calls, [dict(files=['https://e.com/']), dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/'])])
c, calls = fake_purge(dict(prefixes=[refused]))
test_eq((c.purge('z', prefixes=['e.com/s/']), calls), ([dict(purge_everything=True)], [dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/']), dict(purge_everything=True)]))
c, calls = fake_purge(dict(prefixes=[refused]))
test_fail(lambda: c.purge('z', prefixes=['e.com/s/'], fallback_all=False), contains='not on this plan')
test_fail(lambda: fake_purge()[0].purge('z'), contains='purge needs')
test_eq(fake_purge()[0].purge('z', everything=True), [dict(purge_everything=True)])


# a refused prefixes purge after a files purge reports both; rate limits and timeouts retry with backoff; any other error raises
c, calls = fake_purge(dict(prefixes=[refused]))
test_eq(c.purge('z', prefixes=['e.com/s/'], files=['https://e.com/']), [dict(files=['https://e.com/']), dict(purge_everything=True)])
waits, slow = [], lambda: cf_err(RateLimitError, 429, 1134, 'Unable to purge, rate limit reached')
with mock.patch('time.sleep', waits.append):
    c, calls = fake_purge(dict(prefixes=[slow, lambda: APITimeoutError(_rq)]))
    test_eq((c.purge('z', prefixes=['e.com/s/']), calls), ([dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/'])], [dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/'])] * 3))
    test_eq(waits, [1, 2])
    c, calls = fake_purge(dict(prefixes=[slow] * 4))
    test_fail(lambda: c.purge('z', prefixes=['e.com/s/'], tries=3), contains='rate limit')
    test_eq(len(calls), 3)   # no purge of everything after a rate limit
    c, calls = fake_purge(dict(prefixes=[lambda: cf_err(BadRequestError, 400, 1092, 'bad prefix'), lambda: 0]))
    test_fail(lambda: c.purge('z', prefixes=['https://e.com/s/']), contains='bad prefix')
    c, calls = fake_purge(dict(prefixes=[lambda: RuntimeError('socket closed'), lambda: 0]))
    test_fail(lambda: c.purge('z', prefixes=['e.com/s/']), contains='socket closed')
    test_eq(calls, [dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/'])])


# purge reaches the SDK only through `_c`, so a stand-in for `CF` that binds `purge` alone still purges
from unittest.mock import MagicMock
m, sent = MagicMock(), []
m._c = NS(cache=NS(purge=lambda zone_id, **kw: sent.append(kw)))
test_eq((CF.purge(m, 'z', prefixes=['e.com/s/']), sent), ([dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/'])], [dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/'])]))

A zone keeps its cache rules and its custom firewall rules in rulesets, one entrypoint ruleset per phase. ruleset_upsert puts your rules into the entrypoint for phase and keeps every rule there that it does not own, with all its keys, such as logging or ratelimit; only Cloudflare’s read-only version, last_updated and categories are left out of the update. A rule is matched by its ref, so give each rule a stable ref. When the rules with those refs already match yours on the usual keys and every key your rules set, it sends nothing and returns False; otherwise it writes the merged list and returns True. Running it on every deploy is safe. The token needs Zone -> Cache Rules -> Edit for the cache phase, and Zone -> Zone WAF -> Edit for http_request_firewall_custom.
purge empties the zone’s cache by URL files, by URL prefixes, or everything. Files and prefixes go in separate requests, files first, because the API takes one kind per request. A rate limit (HTTP 429 or Cloudflare’s code 1134) or a timeout is retried up to tries times in all, waiting wait seconds and doubling the wait each time. Some plans or tokens refuse a prefix purge, with HTTP 403 or a 400 that names the plan or a permission. With fallback_all=True, the default, such a refusal becomes a purge of everything. Any other error, including a rate limit that outlasts the retries, raises and purges nothing more. The return value lists the purge requests that succeeded: after a fallback, the files purge when it ran first, then the purge of everything, so a caller can tell when the fallback ran.

def purge(
    zid, prefixes:NoneType=None, files:NoneType=None, everything:bool=False, fallback_all:bool=True, tries:int=4,
    wait:int=1
)->list:
Purge the zone cache by files, prefixes or everything, retrying rate limits and timeouts, and purging everything when Cloudflare refuses a partial purge and fallback_all; returns the purges that succeeded.

def ruleset_upsert(
    zid, rules, phase:str='http_request_cache_settings'
)->bool:
Put rules in the zone entrypoint for phase, replacing the rules with the same ref and keeping the rest whole; False when nothing changed.



def fake_rules(rules=()):
    c, calls = CF('x'), []
    R = lambda d: NS(model_dump=lambda exclude_none=True: d)
    c._c = NS(rulesets=NS(phases=NS(get=lambda ph, zone_id: NS(rules=[R(r) for r in rules]),
                                    update=lambda ph, zone_id, rules: calls.append((ph, rules)))))
    return c, calls

import httpx
from unittest import mock
from cloudflare import APITimeoutError, BadRequestError, PermissionDeniedError, RateLimitError
_rq = httpx.Request('POST', 'https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/zones/z/purge_cache')
def cf_err(cls, status, code, msg): return cls(msg, response=httpx.Response(status, request=_rq), body=dict(errors=[dict(code=code, message=msg)]))
refused = lambda: cf_err(PermissionDeniedError, 403, 10000, 'not on this plan')
def fake_purge(fails=None):
    'A client whose purge raises, for each kind of purge in `fails`, the errors listed there in turn, then succeeds; `calls` records each request.'
    c, calls, fails = CF('x'), [], {k: list(v) for k, v in (fails or {}).items()}
    def purge(zone_id, **kw):
        calls.append(kw)
        if (q := fails.get(first(kw))) and (e := q.pop(0)()): raise e
    c._c = NS(cache=NS(purge=purge))
    return c, calls

c, calls = fake_purge()
test_eq(c.purge('z', prefixes=['e.com/s/'], files=['https://e.com/']), [dict(files=['https://e.com/']), dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/'])])
test_eq(calls, [dict(files=['https://e.com/']), dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/'])])
c, calls = fake_purge(dict(prefixes=[refused]))
test_eq((c.purge('z', prefixes=['e.com/s/']), calls), ([dict(purge_everything=True)], [dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/']), dict(purge_everything=True)]))
c, calls = fake_purge(dict(prefixes=[refused]))
test_fail(lambda: c.purge('z', prefixes=['e.com/s/'], fallback_all=False), contains='not on this plan')
test_fail(lambda: fake_purge()[0].purge('z'), contains='purge needs')
test_eq(fake_purge()[0].purge('z', everything=True), [dict(purge_everything=True)])


# a refused prefixes purge after a files purge reports both; rate limits and timeouts retry with backoff; any other error raises
c, calls = fake_purge(dict(prefixes=[refused]))
test_eq(c.purge('z', prefixes=['e.com/s/'], files=['https://e.com/']), [dict(files=['https://e.com/']), dict(purge_everything=True)])
waits, slow = [], lambda: cf_err(RateLimitError, 429, 1134, 'Unable to purge, rate limit reached')
with mock.patch('time.sleep', waits.append):
    c, calls = fake_purge(dict(prefixes=[slow, lambda: APITimeoutError(_rq)]))
    test_eq((c.purge('z', prefixes=['e.com/s/']), calls), ([dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/'])], [dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/'])] * 3))
    test_eq(waits, [1, 2])
    c, calls = fake_purge(dict(prefixes=[slow] * 4))
    test_fail(lambda: c.purge('z', prefixes=['e.com/s/'], tries=3), contains='rate limit')
    test_eq(len(calls), 3)   # no purge of everything after a rate limit
    c, calls = fake_purge(dict(prefixes=[lambda: cf_err(BadRequestError, 400, 1092, 'bad prefix'), lambda: 0]))
    test_fail(lambda: c.purge('z', prefixes=['https://e.com/s/']), contains='bad prefix')
    c, calls = fake_purge(dict(prefixes=[lambda: RuntimeError('socket closed'), lambda: 0]))
    test_fail(lambda: c.purge('z', prefixes=['e.com/s/']), contains='socket closed')
    test_eq(calls, [dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/'])])


# purge reaches the SDK only through `_c`, so a stand-in for `CF` that binds `purge` alone still purges
from unittest.mock import MagicMock
m, sent = MagicMock(), []
m._c = NS(cache=NS(purge=lambda zone_id, **kw: sent.append(kw)))
test_eq((CF.purge(m, 'z', prefixes=['e.com/s/']), sent), ([dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/'])], [dict(prefixes=['e.com/s/'])]))

Helpers
repo_root returns the top folder of the git repository you are working in, found by walking up from the current directory until it finds a .git entry. It returns None outside a repository.
cfeasy ships a SKILL.md file that tells coding agents such as Claude Code how to use the library. mv_skill_md copies it into a project’s .agents/skills/cfeasy/ and .claude/skills/cfeasy/ folders, where those agents look for skills. By default it only prints where it would copy the file; pass dry_run=False to copy it. The project root is dir if you give one, otherwise the repository root, otherwise the current directory.
